Descriptive source: "វិធានការជីវសុវត្ថិភាព ដើម្បីបង្ការជំងឺផ្សាយបក្សី និងជំងឺបក្សីដទៃទៀត សៀវភៅណែនាំសំរាប់កសិកម្មចិញ្ចឹមបក្សីជាលក្ខណៈគ្រួសារ" (Biosecurity Measures to Prevent Avian Influenza and Other Poultry Diseases), FAO / USAID / MAFF, June 2009, Appendix 1 (protocol for cleaning and disinfection).
text:
This source's appendix sets out a cleaning-and-disinfection (C&D) protocol for poultry housing, built around four goals: (1) clean every area where birds are or were kept, with no exceptions; (2) clean thoroughly enough that no dirt is visible to the naked eye; (3) reduce the pathogen load to the lowest practically achievable level through proper disinfection; and (4) only bring in replacement birds from clean, trusted sources so new stock doesn't reintroduce the virus or other disease agents.

Recommended process order:
1. Remove all birds from the area before starting.
2. It's best to clean when the house is empty of birds.
3. Remove loose litter/bedding.
4. Take out equipment that cannot itself be properly cleaned and disinfected in place (e.g. feeders, waterers) so it can be cleaned separately.

How to clean: this source stresses that disinfectant cannot work through visible dirt or dust - physical cleaning has to happen first. The goal of the cleaning step itself is to physically remove dust, dirt, manure, and other visible material. Sweep out loose dust and debris first, then wash surfaces with water and detergent/soap, paying attention to corners, joints, and other spots where dirt collects both inside and outside the housing. This source distinguishes two general categories of cleaning agents: alkaline-based cleaners (suited to organic soiling) and acid-based cleaners (suited to mineral/scale-type soiling).

Disinfection: after cleaning, disinfectant can be applied by spraying, foaming, or fogging, and contact time with the surface matters for how effective it is. This source states that thorough physical cleaning with water and detergent accounts for the great majority of pathogen reduction on a surface, with disinfectant then addressing what physical cleaning leaves behind - meaning a rushed or incomplete cleaning step undermines the disinfection step no matter how strong the disinfectant is.

Honesty note: this source's text includes some specific percentage figures for how much pathogen load different cleaning steps remove, but the figures in the available copy are inconsistent/partially garbled (conflicting numbers appear for what should likely be the same claim). Rather than guess at the intended exact percentages, this entry reports the qualitative point only - thorough physical cleaning before disinfecting is the single most important step - and flags that a cleaner copy of this source would be needed to confirm the precise numbers.
